analysis.one_liner: Strengthens safety rules, slows line speeds, and restricts punishing attendance policies for meatpacking workers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 7 cosponsors, all Democrats or one allied independent, referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, and never received a hearing, amendment, or vote before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have tightened safety rules for the roughly half-million people who work in meat and poultry plants: it restricted fast line speeds that drive injuries, limited "no-fault" attendance systems that give workers demerit points for using legally protected sick leave, required new OSHA standards on ergonomics and infectious disease, and funded more workplace inspectors. It also restored country-of-origin labels on beef, pork, and dairy and added antitrust-style rules aimed at the largest meatpackers.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at federally inspected meat and poultry processing plants gain the most: the bill cited findings that these workers suffer double the private-industry amputation rate and musculoskeletal injuries that can exceed 50 percent of workers [S3]. It would have given them enforceable rights to bathroom breaks without punishment [S3], protection from being fired for refusing dangerous work [S3], a 90-day presumption of retaliation after they raise safety concerns [S3], and damages including attorneys' fees if they sue [S3]. The attendance-policy title covers workers economy-wide, not just in meat plants [S3]. Ranchers and poultry growers gain from limits on packers' spot-market purchases and new rights to recover attorneys' fees under the Packers and Stockyards Act [S3]. Shoppers gain mandatory country-of-origin labels for beef, pork, and dairy [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Meatpacking plant workers, ranchers, and shoppers

how_it_helps.text: Restricts employer attendance systems that assign demerit points for absences, requiring written policies, detail on legally protected leave laws, and a process to challenge wrongly assessed points, with employees able to sue for lost wages, damages, and attorneys' fees [S2, S3].

Blocks the Agriculture Department from issuing line-speed waivers unless a safety official certifies the increase would not harm workers, and bars federal funds from being used on any policy that speeds up slaughter lines [S2, S3].

Directs OSHA to write ergonomic standards for meat and poultry plants, an infectious-disease standard, and a 7-day emergency COVID-19 standard, verifies that workers can use toilets without punishment or sign-out delays, and appropriates $60 million per year from fiscal 2024 through 2029 to hire additional inspectors [S2, S3].

Beefs up anti-retaliation law for meat and poultry workers: a 90-day unrebuttable presumption of retaliation after protected activity, explicit protection against employers threatening to report workers' immigration status, and a private right of action allowing suits with compensatory and punitive damages [S3].

Requires grant recipients for new meat and poultry plants to sign labor peace agreements with unions, bars recipients from selling facilities to packers with more than 10 percent market share, and expands funding for regional and local food systems, including $500 million for the Local Agriculture Market Program in fiscal 2024 [S2, S3].
Restores mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef and pork and extends it to dairy products, so shoppers can see where their meat comes from [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry processing companies bear the main costs: slower permitted line speeds, ergonomic and infectious-disease compliance, bathroom-access and recordkeeping requirements, exposure to private lawsuits with punitive damages, and restrictions on spot-market livestock purchases and sales to dominant packers [S3]. Federal taxpayers fund the new spending — $60 million a year for OSHA inspectors through fiscal 2029, $100 million in processing grants through fiscal 2032, and $500 million for local food-system programs in fiscal 2024 [S3]. Grocery and meat retailers also take on country-of-origin labeling compliance [S2, S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Meatpacking companies, large packers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall hardest on operators' margins: ergonomic programs, on-site occupational medicine, infectious-disease control plans, and slower line speeds all require new spending, and smaller plants with thin margins could struggle to meet the same standards as large companies [S3].

The bill ordered a COVID-19 emergency standard within just 7 days of enactment and expressly exempted it from the Regulatory Flexibility Act, the Paperwork Reduction Act, and executive orders 12866 and 13771 — bypassing the normal cost-benefit review that applies to most federal rules [S3].

The private right of action lets anyone aggrieved by any failure to comply with the OSH Act or this bill sue for compensatory and punitive damages with fees and expert costs, which critics would say invites litigation over technical violations rather than actual harm [S3].

The line-speed provision strips the Agriculture Department of authority to run any program that increases line speeds during the covered period, even where the agency might judge an increase safe, which poultry companies said constrains plant efficiency and processing capacity [S3].

The bill appropriated roughly $940 million in new mandatory spending over the decade — $360 million for OSHA inspectors, $100 million in processing grants, and $500 million for market programs — added to the deficit rather than offset [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and aimed at a workforce the bill's own findings describe as suffering double the private-sector amputation rate and musculoskeletal injuries in more than half of workers [S3]. The costs — compliance spending by processors and about $940 million in appropriations over a decade — are real but modest next to the stakes for worker safety, and the industry-facing competition provisions (spot-market limits, labor peace agreements, market-share restrictions) come at the expense of the largest packers rather than the public [S3]. The genuine weaknesses are procedural: the 7-day emergency COVID standard with normal regulatory review switched off, and a broad private right of action that could generate litigation beyond serious violations [S3]. On balance the bill is a well-targeted worker-protection measure whose largest costs land on a concentrated industry.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Agriculture Committee for the entire two-year Congress — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the bill on February 2, 2023, joined by original cosponsors Gillibrand, Blumenthal, Sanders, Warren, and Schatz [S1, S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S5].
Seven senators cosponsored — six Democrats and one independent — and no Republican signed on [S4].
The action record shows no committee hearing, no markup, no vote, and no floor action at any point through the end of the 118th Congress in January 2025 [S5, S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry processing companies are better off because the bill died: no line-speed limits, no ergonomic or infectious-disease standards, no attendance-policy restrictions, no new private lawsuits, and no new competition rules for the largest packers. The members who supported it gained a public position but no policy change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Meatpacking companies that avoided new safety rules

sides.party_line_note: All eight supporters were Democrats plus one allied independent; no Republican ever cosponsored, and the bill never reached a vote where a partisan split could be recorded.

industries.note: The bill's core targets: line-speed limits, ergonomic and infectious-disease standards, mandatory bathroom access, restrictions on point-based attendance systems, retaliation protections, and private lawsuits with punitive damages. Its safety gains for a heavily immigrant, low-wage workforce come directly at these companies' operating costs.

industries.industry: Large meat packers with dominant market share
industries.note: Title II amends the Packers and Stockyards Act to restrict packers' spot-market livestock purchases, adds definitions and unlawful-practice provisions, and bars grant-funded plants from being sold to or merged with any packer holding more than 10 percent of the market — rules aimed directly at the biggest firms.

New meat and poultry plants could only receive federal processing grants if they signed labor peace agreements: no interference with organizing, workplace access for organizers, and recognition upon majority sign-up.

Restoring mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef, pork, and dairy adds supply-chain tracking and labeling compliance, in exchange for giving shoppers origin information the voluntary regime does not guarantee.

The bill appropriated $60 million a year through fiscal 2029 for additional inspectors and created a permanent regional emphasis inspection program for meat and poultry plants, expanding the agency's reach into workplaces it has historically covered thinly.
